title: Kenyan Chicken Biryani
community: Swahili and Indian-Kenyan — a coastal celebration centrepiece
author: Chef Amina Hassan
desc: Kenyan Chicken Biryani — fragrant basmati rice layered with spiced chicken, caramelised onions, saffron, and aromatic spices, then sealed and slow-cooked until the rice absorbs all the fragrance and colour. Kenya's most luxurious rice dish.
longDesc: Biryani occupies a special place in Kenyan coastal cooking — it is more elaborate than pilau, more fragrant, and more celebratory. The layering technique — alternating spiced chicken with par-cooked rice and sealing to steam together — gives biryani its characteristic layered colour and the way each grain of rice carries both fragrance and richness. On the Kenyan coast, biryani is the dish of weddings and Eid.
ingredients: 2 cups basmati rice — soaked 30 minutes, rinsed
Pinch of saffron soaked in 3 tbsp warm milk — optional
2 tsp biryani masala or curry powder
steps: Marinate chicken in yogurt, garlic, ginger, biryani masala, turmeric, paprika, and salt for 1 hour.
Par-cook rice: boil in well-salted water with cardamom, cinnamon, cloves, and cumin for 6—7 minutes until 70% cooked. Drain.
Fry onions until deeply golden — 15 minutes. Reserve half for garnish.
In the pot, cook the marinated chicken in oil over medium heat with half the fried onions and tomatoes until the chicken is almost cooked — 20—25 minutes.
Layer par-cooked rice over the chicken. Drizzle saffron milk over the rice.
Scatter mint, coriander, and remaining fried onions over the rice.
Seal the pot tightly with foil, then the lid. Cook on the lowest possible heat for 25—30 minutes (the dum cooking stage).
Remove from heat. Rest sealed for 10 minutes before opening.
Gently fold from the bottom to serve — mixing the layers slightly.
chefTips: The dum (sealed steam) cooking stage is what makes biryani unique — do not unseal during this time.
Par-cook the rice only 70% — it finishes in the dum stage.
Deeply fried onions are not optional — they provide sweetness and body to the dish.
A heavy pot with a tight-fitting lid gives the best dum result.
commonMistakes: Fully cooking the rice before layering — it becomes mushy in the dum stage.
Lifting the lid during dum cooking — releases the steam that finishes the rice.
Not using a heavy pot — a thin pot creates hot spots and burns the bottom.

faqs.a: Dum (from the Persian word for breath) is a sealed cooking technique where food cooks in its own steam in a tightly sealed pot. The gentle steam permeates the layers evenly, cooking the rice while infusing it with all the flavours below.

faqs.q: What is the difference between biryani and pilau?
faqs.a: Pilau cooks the rice and meat together in one stage. Biryani layers par-cooked rice over cooked meat and finishes with sealed steam (dum cooking). Biryani is more complex, more aromatic, and more celebratory.

cookingScience: Dum cooking creates a closed system where the limited water in the pot converts to steam, cooking the rice uniformly from all sides simultaneously. The sealed lid maintains pressure slightly above atmospheric, raising the boiling point marginally and producing more evenly cooked rice than open-pot methods.
sustainabilityTips: Make a large pot — biryani is ideal for feeding many people efficiently from one cooking session.
storage: Refrigerate for up to 2 days — best eaten fresh.
reheating: Sprinkle with water and reheat gently in a sealed pot.
healthBenefits: Good source of protein and B vitamins.
Saffron contains crocin — a powerful antioxidant.
Yogurt marinade tenderises and adds probiotics.
culturalNote: Chicken biryani is one of the most celebratory dishes in Kenyan coastal cuisine — prepared for weddings, Eid, and special family occasions. Its elaborate preparation is itself a mark of respect for the occasion and the guests being honoured.
regionalVariations: Mombasa-style biryani — rich with ghee and saffron.
Lamu-style biryani — with rose water for fragrance.
